cost.notes:
I built tonight's passage index on my desktop. The estimate here comes from the steady part of the run. In real time it took six and a half hours, including a memory spill and a crash. I could go and make tea while that job ran. I'd rather my users didn't have time to do the same.

[Point to the grey field of passages and the grey term.] I take the number of passages and multiply by what it costs to encode one. That's the work I've already done for this index. [Follow the red queries into the field, then point to the red term.] As requests arrive, I count the queries so far. For each fresh query I pay to make its vector and then search the index. The total is what I spent encoding the passages plus what I've spent serving queries.

If an agent calls search several times to answer one question, those encodes can all sit on the path to the answer. I wanted to make that part cheaper. What else could search the passage vectors I'd already paid to make?

zero-mech.notes:
[Read the flight query. Point to the row for "cheap".] I run Stella's tokenizer to turn the text into token IDs. Each ID gets me a row from the table. I unpack the stored integer rows when I load the model, so the query can fetch rows that are already in memory.

[Follow the single arrow to Zero's vector.] I take a weighted mean of those rows, then normalize the vector. The weight is the square root of the token count. If I type "cheap" again, it gets a little more weight. Each repeat adds less than the one before it. Once I've done that, the vector is ready to search against the same passages.

[Point to Zero's vector beside Stella's.] For this query I get a cosine of 0.88 with Stella. Nano gets 0.96 on the same text. That tells me how closely the vectors point in the same direction for this one query. What I'd like to know is whether the encoder can tell which way I'm flying. Let's keep the words and reverse the trip.

order.notes:
[Read the two routes. Pause between them.] If I mix up Paris to Rome and Rome to Paris, I'm at the wrong airport. To Zero, those queries have the same tokens with the same counts. It looks up the same rows, gives them the same weights, and makes exactly the same vector. Both directions get the same ranking.

[Point to the zoomed axis, then to Stella at 0.9964 and Nano at 0.9991.] I've zoomed right in near one. Each marker gives the median cosine across the reversals. Stella moves a little, Nano moves even less, and Zero sits at exactly one. A small change can be enough to swap two passages that were close in score.

I checked the first result in both directions for 24 pairs. Stella got both right on four pairs, Nano on two, and Zero on none. If routes matter to my users, I'd put both directions in the test set and judge them separately. That gap between pointing the right way and putting the right passage first mattered when I trained Zero.

worst.notes:
I thought I'd start with the best retriever and give myself the best shot at a good lookup table. [Trace the gte-large line from left to right.] Each line starts with the model searching its own index. It ends with a table I fitted to that model and tested on the same index. gte-large came first with its own query encoder and tenth with its table.

[Trace Stella's line.] Stella went from second to first. Its table still scored lower than Stella's own query encoder.

If I were choosing a model for a new index, I'd make a small index for each candidate. Then I'd fit a table and score both query encoders against the same relevance judgments. Those fits took minutes on an A100. I'd rather spend those minutes before I commit to encoding the whole corpus. With Stella's index fixed, I also wanted a cheaper encoder that could use word order. That's the job I gave Nano.

recovery.notes:
[Point to the leftmost Stella point and the rightmost Zero point. Pause so the room can find both.] I kept the links between passages fixed. Changing the query vector changes which passages look promising as the search follows those links. Turning up ef lets the search explore more of the graph. Here Zero still recovers a smaller share of its own exact top 10 at the widest setting than Stella does at the narrowest.

I saw a need for wider search with uncompressed vectors as well. In the paper's test of 25 models on TREC-COVID and FiQA, the median lookup table needed ef 256 to match its teacher at 64. Match here means recover the same share. Each encoder has its own exact top 10 to check against.

I also measured how much nDCG each encoder lost relative to its own exact search. On TREC-COVID, only 12 of the 25 tables needed a wider search to match the teacher's loss. Finding one more exact neighbour can leave the first useful result right where it was. Before I pay for a wider search, I want to know what it does for the results someone would open.

I brought a few queries to try on this shard. Let's look at the pages the rankers return and see what changes when I widen the search.

recipe.notes:
[Point to the two constraints.] I'd agree on a relevance floor and a tail latency budget before I tune anything. Then I'd look for the lowest end-to-end median among the settings that meet both. The encoder, ef, and oversampling are one decision. The cheapest encoder can send me off to do more search work.

I'd start by sampling real queries from my traffic and judging which passages answer them. Then I'd run exact search with each encoder on the same index and score nDCG@10. That tells me how each encoder ranks my passages before I ask the graph to find them. If the exact results miss my floor, I'd look at those rankings before spending time on a sweep.

For the sweep I'd vary ef and oversampling. I'd time encoding and search together and record both the median and the p95. Of the combinations that pass, I'd ship the one with the lowest median. Its ef and oversampling go with it. I'd check that configuration again at the load I expect to serve.

You need 0.55 nDCG@10 and a 3 ms p95. Which encoder ships?

solved.notes:
[Keep the table off screen. Ask this if the room has yet to hear the question.] You need 0.55 nDCG@10 and a 3 ms p95. Which encoder ships?

[Give the room and Zoom time to answer. Reveal the table and point to the middle row.] I'd ship Nano at ef 64. Its p95 was 2.12 milliseconds. That's for encoding and search together on tonight's index.

[Point to the first row, then the last.] If I can live with 0.50, I'd ship Zero at ef 512. Its p95 was 0.96 milliseconds, even with that wider search. Raise the floor to 0.62 and every tested setting misses a requirement. Only Stella reaches that floor, and its p95 is 34.6 milliseconds. At that point I'd ask the team which limit it can move.

I ran the sweep sequentially on this laptop, with oversampling fixed at four. To try this on my own traffic, I can keep one set of passage vectors and swap the query encoder. Here's the FastEmbed example I'd start with.

close.notes:
[Point to Qdrant/stella-en-400M-v5-doc-onnx in the editor.] I'd use Stella's document model to embed the passages and upload those vectors once. [Move to Qdrant/constella-zero, then point to the collection name in the query call.] When a question comes in, Zero makes the query vector and I search the same collection. If I want to try Nano, I swap the model on that line. I can send it the same questions and see which passages move up or down.

[Point to the install command.] I'd install FastEmbed 0.9.0 or later with pip. The first thing I'd do on Monday is pull a batch of real queries and judge which passages I'd want back.

[Advance to the thank-you slide. Leave the QR codes up for questions.]
